name: Sikh Empire (Lahore Durbar)

areaKm2.note: Infobox 520,000 km2 in 1839; text: over 200,000 sq mi at its zenith (Amarpal Singh 2010, Barczewski 2016 p. 89, Khilnani 1972 p. 251, via the article). Low: the conservative 260,124 km2 the article cites; Lafont 2003 gives 390,000 km2. High: the world_1800 Sikhs polygon (about 526,000 km2 on the sphere), which covers Lahore, Peshawar and Kashmir; no later basemap draws the Sikh state.

population.note: Mid: about 12 million (Pashaura Singh, The Encyclopedia of Empire 2016, via the article). Low: about 5.35 million in 1838 (Herrli, The Coins of the Sikhs p. 10). High: 15 million (Lafont 2003 p. 131). Amarinder Singh 2010 p. 23 gives 3.5 million for 1831, so the estimates span a factor of four; no census was taken. Cross-check: OWID Pakistan 1840 = 14.6M for all of modern Pakistan, which includes Sindh and Baluchistan outside the empire.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: Lahore, Amritsar, Multan, Peshawar, Srinagar and Jammu were large trading and garrison towns in an agrarian province; no city counts were found for the 1840s. Close to the Maratha 1760 snapshot (0.09).

activePersonnel.note: Standing Khalsa army in late 1845. Mid: Amarpal Singh's breakdown (Sidhu 2010 p. 36, via the article) 53,576 regular infantry + 6,235 regular cavalry + 16,292 irregular cavalry + 10,698 gunners = 86,801. Low: over 80,000 in 1845 (Hernon 2003 p. 547). High: Smith 2019 pp. 45-50 gives about 153,000 regular and irregular, of which 55,000 jagirdari levies (counted as trainedReserves), leaving about 98,000.

trainedReserves.note: Jagirdari fauj (feudal levies of the jagirdars, raised on call): 55,000 (Smith 2019 pp. 45-50, via the article) (high); the Sikh Khalsa Army article gives 50,000-52,000 irregulars for 1838-39 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Khalsa_Army). Fort garrisons (Fauj-i-Kilajat, 50-250 men per fort) are not counted; no total was found.

supportPersonnel.note: 10,698 gunners (Amarpal Singh, Sidhu 2010 p. 36, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Sikh_War) plus a few hundred engineers and staff; high adds elephant, camel and bullock drivers of the gun train (educated guess, no count found).

mobilizationRatio.note: Regional analogy: Mughal Empire 1690 and Maratha 1760 snapshots, Barua 2005 p. 47 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire: the armed peasantry of the north Indian military labour market was about 3% of the population. Low 0.02, high 0.035 as in those snapshots.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Fauj-i-Ain regular infantry battalions (about 800 men each, drilled on French and British lines): 53,576 in 1845 (Amarpal Singh, Sidhu 2010 p. 36, via the article). Low: 45,000 in 1838-39 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Khalsa_Army, uncited there). Smith 2019 puts the whole Fauj-i-Ain (infantry, cavalry, artillery) at 70,000.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: smoothbore flintlock muskets on the British pattern, made in Punjab arsenals; level with East India Company sepoys, behind percussion and rifled arms.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75 (professional standing army). Evidence: long-service paid regulars drilled by Ventura, Allard and Court in battalions and brigades since the 1820s.

count.note: Regular cavalry (dragoons, lancers and Allard's cuirassiers): 6,235 in 1845 (Smith 2019 pp. 45-50 and Sidhu 2010 p. 36, via the article). High: 10,000 regular cavalry in 1838-39 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Khalsa_Army).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: European-style sabres, lances and carbines; smaller horses than British dragoons.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: drilled regulars, but the cavalry was the weak arm of the Khalsa and did little at Mudki and Ferozeshah.

count.note: Irregular cavalry (ghorchurras, Fauj-i-sowar): 16,292 (Amarpal Singh, Sidhu 2010 p. 36) to 22,000 (Smith 2019 pp. 45-50), both via the article.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: own horses and mixed arms (matchlocks, swords, lances).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: experienced horsemen of the misl tradition, not drilled in formation.

count.note: 381 guns plus 388 swivel guns (zamburaks) in 1845 (Smith 2019 pp. 45-50, via the article); swivel guns are not counted as pieces. Low: 182 heavy guns, 20 howitzers and 60 light guns in 1838-39 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Khalsa_Army). The British took 69 guns in the four battles of the war (infobox).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75 (among the era's best). Evidence: Lahore-cast guns, many of heavier calibre than the British horse and field batteries they faced at Ferozeshah and Sobraon.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: gunners trained under Court and Gardner; accurate fire at Mudki and Ferozeshah.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: after Ranjit Singh's death (1839) the army was run by regimental panchayats; the commanders Lal Singh and Tej Singh failed to press the advantage at Ferozeshah and are widely held to have betrayed it.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75 (professional with strong unit identity). Evidence: Khalsa religious and regimental identity; the Sobraon entrenchment held until it was overrun.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: army that forced the war on the Durbar and crossed the Sutlej in December 1845; offset by pay arrears and distrust of its own commanders.

weapons.note: Anchor: 6 (1805, flintlock musket, 12-pdr gun). Evidence: flintlock muskets and smoothbore field and siege guns; no percussion or rifled arms in quantity.

armor.note: Anchor: 5-6 (half-armour to none/cuirass). Evidence: Allard's cuirassiers and some mail in the irregular horse; infantry unarmoured.

ships.note: Anchor: 3-4 (oared river craft). Evidence: river boats and ferries on the Indus and the five rivers only; no warships.

fortification.note: Anchor: 5 (trace italienne) to 6 (Vauban-type). Evidence: Lahore and Multan forts, Mughal-era walled towns, field entrenchments at Ferozeshah and Sobraon.

logistics.note: Anchor: 5 (magazines). Evidence: arsenals and magazines at Lahore; elephant, camel, horse and ox draught for the guns; no railway.

communications.note: Anchor: 5 (couriers). Evidence: mounted couriers and newswriters; no telegraph in Punjab.

isr.note: Anchor: 5. Evidence: irregular-cavalry scouting and spies.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 India 1841 = 944, 1850 = 947 (2011 int$). Punjab has no own series (Pakistan starts 1950); the India value is used, band about +/-10%.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. State revenue in 1844 was about Rs 3.49 crore (land revenue 3.25 crore incl. 0.95 crore of jagirs, customs 0.24 crore; Cunningham 1849 p. 424, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Empire), and the paid Khalsa took most of the treasury's cash; the share of output is not documented.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Textiles (Kashmir shawls), arms and craft production; the Maratha 1760 snapshot's 0.15 (Mughal-era structure, Moosvi 18% for the 16th century) assumed.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Inundation-canal and well-irrigated grain farming of the doabs; the army was fed from local markets.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. The Mughal imperial road (Grand Trunk route) Lahore-Attock-Peshawar and the Lahore-Multan road; the rest were unmetalled tracks.

railKm.note: The first passenger railway in India ran in 1853 (Bombay-Thane, 34 km); none existed in Punjab in 1845.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: landlocked; Indus river landings only (Sindh and Karachi were British from 1843).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: no seagoing merchant fleet.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. A magazine-supplied regular army with a heavy gun train, operating close to its own frontier on the Sutlej.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess, about 5% of the population (Maratha 1760 snapshot ratio ~6.7%): plough bullocks, camels, horses and the army's gun elephants.

chokepoints: Pir Panjal and Banihal passes to Kashmir

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: familiar terrain, local supply and fortified Lahore and Multan; a ruling Sikh minority over a mostly Muslim population limits population support, so below the full 1.2 row.

notes: Snapshot = December 1845, when the Khalsa crossed the Sutlej and the First Anglo-Sikh War began. Personnel: the paid Fauj-i-Ain regulars (infantry, regular cavalry, artillery) and the irregular ghorchurra cavalry are activePersonnel; jagirdari levies are trainedReserves; fort garrisons are not counted. Army figures via the First Anglo-Sikh War article (Smith 2019, Sidhu 2010/Amarpal Singh, Hernon 2003); the sources differ by 10-20% and the 1838-39 figures of the Sikh Khalsa Army article are uncited there. Population is the weakest value: estimates run from 3.5 million (1831) to 15 million, mid 12 million. Territory = everything inside the world_1800 Sikhs polygon (Punjab, Multan, Peshawar, Kashmir, Jammu); includes is empty. Economy and logistics values other than GDP per capita are educated guesses.
